stops.name: Sesenheim, Friederike Brion at the parsonage
stops.campa: Riding out into Alsace he comes to the pastor's house at Sesenheim and loves at once the pastor's daughter Friederike Brion, with her fair braids and country grace, as if stepped from a Goldsmith idyll. Through this happiness pour the songs that free German lyric forever: Willkommen und Abschied, Mailied, the Heidenröslein, where feeling and landscape become one breath. But when his study ends he rides away and does not return; the guilt of having wounded her he will confess as a wound in himself for years.
stops.quote: Es schlug mein Herz, geschwind zu Pferde! / Es war getan fast eh gedacht.

stops.name: Frankfurt: Götz von Berlichingen and the Storm
stops.campa: Home again as a young advocate, he writes in a few weeks, in defiant Shakespearean freedom, the drama of Götz von Berlichingen with the Iron Hand: the honest robber-knight of the old Empire crushed between princes and law. Its raw energy, its scorn of French unities, its cry of liberty make it the manifesto of a generation. Overnight the unknown lawyer is the leader of the young poets of Germany. Götz's parting curse becomes a proverb in every mouth.

stops.name: Wetzlar and Frankfurt: Charlotte Buff and Werther
stops.campa: At Wetzlar, on his legal training, he loves hopelessly the betrothed Charlotte Buff; and when his friend Jerusalem shoots himself over another man's wife, the two griefs fuse. In four weeks of fever he writes The Sorrows of Young Werther: the letters of a soul that loves, suffers, and dies by its own hand. The little book sets all Europe weeping; young men dress in the blue coat and yellow waistcoat, and some follow Werther into the grave. Napoleon carries it through seven campaigns. The unknown German is suddenly the most famous author alive.

stops.name: Frankfurt, the great hymns of genius (Prometheus)
stops.campa: In the same storming years pour from him the free-rhythmed hymns of Titanic self-assertion: Wandrers Sturmlied, Ganymed, and above all Prometheus, where the chained fire-bringer defies Zeus and the whole heaven of gods, and swears to sit and form men in his own image, a race to suffer and rejoice and heed the immortals no more than he. The poem, unpublished but passed hand to hand, is read as sheer blasphemy and sheer liberation, and helps ignite the pantheism-quarrel of the age.
stops.quote: Hier sitz ich, forme Menschen / Nach meinem Bilde, / Ein Geschlecht, das mir gleich sei.

stops.name: Frankfurt: Lili Schönemann and the broken engagement
stops.campa: Famous now, courted, restless, he becomes engaged to Lili Schönemann, a banker's beautiful daughter of the Frankfurt patriciate. He loves her truly, but the elegant world of her circle chafes the poet who longs to be free; the confessional songs to Lili: Neue Liebe, neues Leben, Auf dem See. They record both the sweetness and the sense of a chain. In the very summer of the engagement he flees to Switzerland, to the mountains, to breathe. By autumn the bond quietly breaks; freedom wins, and Weimar calls.
stops.quote: Herz, mein Herz, was soll das geben? / Was bedränget dich so sehr?

stops.name: Weimar, arrival at the court of Duke Karl August
stops.campa: On the strength of Werther the eighteen-year-old Duke Karl August calls him to the small residence of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach, and on 7 November he arrives. What was meant as a visit becomes a life. The two young men ride, hunt, skate and carouse; the scandalized court watches the genius-poet turn statesman. Within a year he sits on the privy council. He takes the little garden-house across the Ilm, and begins to bind his storming spirit to the daily service of a real, if tiny, state.

stops.name: Weimar: Charlotte von Stein
stops.campa: He meets Charlotte von Stein, wife of the master of the horse, seven years his elder, mother of seven, refined and self-possessed. To her over ten years he writes near seventeen hundred letters and notes; she becomes his teacher in tact, restraint and inward form, the noble measure that tames the Titan. It is she, more than any duty, who turns the storm-poet into the classic master. The long, chaste, ardent bond will shape his soul until Italy breaks it.
stops.quote: Warum gabst du uns die tiefen Blicke, / Unsre Zukunft ahndungsvoll zu schaun?
stops.quote_source: Warum gabst du uns die tiefen Blicke (to Charlotte von Stein)

stops.name: Tiefurt and Weimar, the Court of the Muses of Anna Amalia
stops.campa: The Dowager Duchess Anna Amalia, herself learned and musical, has drawn to little Weimar a whole constellation: Wieland the poet, Herder brought to be superintendent, Musäus, Knebel. She holds her Court of the Muses at the summer house of Tiefurt on the Ilm. Goethe writes and acts in the amateur theatricals, plays lovers and fools before the court, composes masques and Singspiele. The small residency of a few thousand souls is becoming, by will and genius, the Athens of the Germans.

stops.name: Ilmenau, the reopening of the silver mines
stops.campa: The Duke sets him over mines, roads, war-commission and treasury. At Ilmenau in the Thuringian forest he labors for years to reopen the drowned silver and copper workings, descending the shafts, studying the strata, wrestling with debt and flood. The venture will in the end fail, the pit collapse; but the mountains teach him geology, and on the plank wall of the Gickelhahn hut above the town he writes in pencil the stillest poem in the language: the wanderer's night-song. Over all the hilltops is peace.
stops.quote: Über allen Gipfeln / ist Ruh, / in allen Wipfeln / spürest du / kaum einen Hauch.

stops.name: Weimar: Iphigenie and the pacified soul
stops.campa: In the midst of his official burdens he writes, first in prose, the drama Iphigenie auf Tauris, and plays Orestes himself before the court. In the Greek priestess who by pure truth and humanity redeems the blood-curse of her house and unbinds the Furies, he has made the very image of his Weimar discipline: the storm within tamed to noble measure, salvation not by the gods' arbitrariness but by the human soul made whole. The Titan of Prometheus has become the healer Iphigenie.
stops.quote: Und eine Stimme hört ich, die da sprach: / Geh, rette den Bedrängten, der dich ruft.

stops.name: Weimar, the discovery of the intermaxillary bone
stops.campa: Bent over skulls in his anatomical study, he finds in the human upper jaw the intermaxillary bone: the little suture that the great anatomists had denied to man to set him apart from the beasts. Goethe proves it present, hidden and fused. To him this is no small triumph but a keystone: man is not exempt from the one great law of forming nature; all is metamorphosis, all is one. In joy he writes to Herder that he has found it, the connexion of all being.
stops.quote: Es soll dir gewiß auch menschlich wohl dabei werden, denn es ist wie ein Schlußstein zum Menschen.

stops.name: Weimar, the granite and the first Faust fragment
stops.campa: In these crowded years of office he studies granite as the oldest, deepest, most enduring of stones, the sober foundation of the earth, and writes of standing upon a naked summit and saying: here on the oldest, first, eternal altar I feel the primal ground of the world. The storming poet has become an observer of nature's slow law. In his desk lies the Urfaust, the earliest scenes of the great drama, still hidden: Gretchen already condemned, the pact not yet struck. The work that will span his whole life waits in the dark.
